title: Likes and dislikes
goal: Say what you like, both things and activities — two different patterns with the same verb — while adding plurals that are also objects.
bekal: form plurals that are also objects: *a könyveket*, *a filmeket*

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Mit szeretsz csinálni?
dialogs.intro: Lunch in the school canteen. Budi's plate is full; Anna's is already empty.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Igen, nagyon szeretem őket. A gulyás a kedvencem.
lines.id: Yes, I like it a lot. Goulash is my favorite.
lines.literal: yes, very I-like-them them-OBJ. the goulash the favorite-my.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: That one I don't like. Too sour.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Én imádom. És mit szeretsz csinálni?
lines.id: I love it. And what do you like doing?
lines.literal: I I-adore-it. and what-OBJ you-like do?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Szeretek focizni és zenét hallgatni. Te?
lines.id: I like playing football and listening to music. You?
lines.literal: I-like to-play-football and music-OBJ to-listen. you?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: Én olvasok és úszom. Utálom a focit.
lines.id: I read and swim. I hate football.
lines.literal: I I-read and I-swim. I-hate-it the football-OBJ.

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.id: It's boring. But I like films.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: What kind of films do you like?

lines.speaker: Anna:
lines.text: A vígjátékokat. A horrort nem szeretem.
lines.id: Comedies. I don't like horror films.
lines.literal: the comedy-PL-OBJ. the horror-OBJ not I-like-it.

notes: **Szeretem and szeretek in one dialogue.** Look at the second and sixth lines. *Szeretem őket* uses the definite form because the object is *őket* — the food is already identified. *Szeretek focizni* uses the indefinite form because the object is not a thing but an **activity**. This is a direct application of the unit 11 rule, and the place where beginners trip most often.

**Milyen filmeket szeretsz? is also indefinite**, even though *filmeket* is plural and an object. The trigger is *milyen* — it asks for a kind, not for one specific film. Compare *A filmeket szeretem*, which is definite because of the *a*.

**A plural object stacks two endings.** *film* → *filmek* (plural) → *filmeket* (plural + object). The order is always the same: plural first, object second. This holds across all of Hungarian and is never reversed.

**A gulyás a kedvencem** puts two nouns face to face with no verb, following the unit 1 rule. Literally "the goulash the my-favorite". The word *kedvenc* can also be an adjective: *a kedvenc ételem* (my favorite food).

**Imád and utál are the ends of the ladder.** *Imádom* means "I love it" and is used every day without sounding over the top, while *utálom* is every bit as strong as "I hate it". For a softer feeling: *nem nagyon szeretem* (I don't really like it).

grammars.title: Two patterns for "like"
body: The verb is the same, the set of endings differs — and what decides it is the form of the object.
after: **The fastest check:** if a word ending in *-ni* follows *szeret*, it's almost certainly the indefinite form. If there's an *a/az*, it's almost certainly the definite form.
*Szeret* also means "love" for people: *Szeretlek* (unit 11) uses the special *-lak/-lek* form, and *Szeretem Annát* uses the definite form because of the proper name.

grammars.title: Plurals that are also objects
body: Two endings stacked, always in the same order.
after: The linking vowel is always *-a-* or *-e-*, following vowel harmony — not *-o-* as in the singular. So *ház* → *házat* (singular) but *házak* → *házakat* (plural).
Remember the unit 3 rule again: **after a number, don't use the plural**. *Két könyvet kérek*, not *két könyveket*.

grammars.title: The ladder of likes and dislikes
body: Five steps that cover almost everything you need to say.
after: There's one more very Hungarian pattern: *Jobban szeretem a teát, mint a kávét* = "I like tea better than coffee". It uses *jobban* from unit 16 and settles every question of choosing.
To ask for an opinion: *Ízlik?* (tasty? — food only) and *Tetszik?* (do you like it? — for anything). Both flip the subject around, so the answer is *Ízlik* or *Tetszik*, not *Ízlem*.

blocks.text: Notice that *zenét hallgat* and *filmet néz* already carry their own objects. When you use them after *szeret*, the object stays inside: *Szeretek zenét hallgatni*. Layered structures like this are what start to make your sentences sound grown-up rather than a list of words.

blocks.text: One sentence that will make anyone happy: *Nagyon finom volt, köszönöm!* — "It was delicious, thank you!". And one more that's honest and still polite if something isn't to your taste: *Érdekes íze van* — "It has an interesting flavor".
